p.src: Preferred Frame, Superluminal Recession, and the Horizon

u.src: Preferred Frame, Superluminal Recession, and the Horizon
en: Preferred Frame, Superluminal Recession, and the Horizon

p.src: The cosmic microwave background does pick out a special frame. In the frame where that radiation looks isotropic, the nearby galaxies are also, on average, at rest. If we move through the background, photons in the forward direction are Doppler shifted to higher energy and photons in the backward direction to lower energy. The preferred frame is the one in which the microwave background looks isotropic, and it is also, on average, the frame in which the local galaxies are at rest.

p.src: A second question concerns recession speeds. Hubble’s law says that sufficiently distant galaxies separate according to $v = H d .$ For large enough $d$, this recession speed exceeds the speed of light. That does not contradict relativity, because the prohibition is local: one object cannot pass another right in front of us faster than light. The statement about distant galaxies is a statement about the geometry between widely separated places.

p.src: The Expanding Metric and the Line Analogy

u.src: The Expanding Metric and the Line Analogy
en: The Expanding Metric and the Line Analogy

p.src: A useful picture is one-dimensional. Imagine a line made of atoms. If we stretch an ordinary material line, eventually it breaks. Now modify the picture: every time neighboring atoms separate too much, we insert another one between them. The line keeps growing, but its local character does not thin out.

p.src: In this picture there is still a local limiting signal speed, just as sound on an ordinary line has a limiting speed. The rule is local: a disturbance cannot outrun that speed relative to nearby points. Nevertheless, if the line is long enough and new points are inserted rapidly enough, sufficiently distant parts of it recede so fast that a signal can never get back.

p.src: Last Scattering and the Observable Universe

u.src: Last Scattering and the Observable Universe
en: Last Scattering and the Observable Universe

p.src: The horizon is the place where recession reaches the speed of light. The surface of last scattering lies slightly inside it. A signal emitted from the horizon would be stretched without bound; the last-scattering radiation has a huge but finite redshift.

p.src: The redshift of the last-scattering radiation is roughly a factor of $10^3$. That is already so large that the surface of last scattering is, for many purposes, very close to the horizon. The observable universe is the portion of the universe from which light can reach us.

p.src:
Now the basic expansion equation is $\left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho ,
\qquad c=1 .$ Here $a(t)$ is the scale factor, and $\rho$ is the total energy density.

p.src:
For matter, $\rho=\frac{\text{const.}}{a^3},
\qquad
a(t)\sim t^{2/3}.$ This is the case of massive objects moving with the overall expansion and essentially at rest in the comoving frame.

\qquad

p.src: Radiation Pressure and Cold Matter

u.src: Radiation Pressure and Cold Matter
en: Radiation Pressure and Cold Matter

p.src: Start with radiation. Consider a one-dimensional box, just a line segment of length $L$, containing photons bouncing back and forth. In one dimension, force and pressure are effectively the same thing.

u.src: Start with radiation. Consider a one-dimensional box, just a line segment of length $L$, containing photons bouncing back and forth. In one dimension, force and pressure are effectively the same thing.
en: Start with radiation. Consider a one-dimensional box, just a line segment of length $L$, containing photons bouncing back and forth. In one dimension, force and pressure are effectively the same thing.

p.src: Take a photon of momentum magnitude $p$. When it reflects from a wall, its momentum changes by $\Delta p = 2p.$ The time between successive collisions with the same wall is $\Delta t = \frac{2L}{c}.$ Therefore the average force on the wall is $F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}=\frac{pc}{L}.$ For a photon, $E=pc,$ so $F=\frac{E}{L}.$ The energy divided by the length is the one-dimensional energy density. In this one-dimensional case, $P=\rho .$

When it reflects from a wall, its momentum changes by $\Delta p = 2p.$ The time between successive collisions with the same wall is $\Delta t = \frac{2L}{c}.$ Therefore the average force on the wall is $F=\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}=\frac{pc}{L}.$ For a photon, $E=pc,$ so $F=\frac{E}{L}.$ The energy divided by the length is the one-dimensional energy density. In this one-dimensional case, $P=\rho .$

In this one-dimensional case, $P=\rho .$

p.src: With many photons the same relation survives after averaging. The total force is just the total energy per unit length.

u.src: With many photons the same relation survives after averaging. The total force is just the total energy per unit length.
en: With many photons the same relation survives after averaging. The total force is just the total energy per unit length.

p.src: Now go to three dimensions. If all photons moved along one axis only, they would exert pressure on one pair of faces and none on the others. That is deliberately wrong, but it shows immediately what has to be corrected. In an isotropic bath, momentum is distributed over all directions. On average, one third of the energy density contributes to each pressure component. The result is $P=\frac{\rho}{3}.$

p.src: The Equation of State

u.src: The Equation of State
en: The Equation of State

p.src:
Pressure is taken to be proportional to energy density, $P=w\rho .$ On the board the same parameter is written as $\omega$. For the two basic cases, $w=0 \quad \text{for cold matter},
\qquad
w=\frac{1}{3} \quad \text{for radiation}.$

p.src: Intermediate cases are possible. Values between $0$ and $1/3$ describe material that is neither completely cold nor fully relativistic. Warm dark matter is the example mentioned here.

p.src: Equation of state $P=\omega\rho$ together with the density-scaling argument.

u.src: Equation of state $P=\omega\rho$ together with the density-scaling argument.

p.src: The next question is whether $w$ controls the dependence of $\rho$ on $a$. The answer comes from a thermodynamic identity.

u.src: The next question is whether $w$ controls the dependence of $\rho$ on $a$. The answer comes from a thermodynamic identity.
en: The next question is whether $w$ controls the dependence of $\rho$ on $a$. The answer comes from a thermodynamic identity.

p.src: Take a box of volume $V$. If the contents exert pressure $P$, then when the box expands by $dV$ the work done on the walls is $dE=-P\,dV.$ Now write the energy as $E=\rho V.$ Its differential is $dE=\rho\,dV+V\,d\rho .$ Equating the two expressions gives $\rho\,dV+V\,d\rho=-P\,dV,$ or $V\,d\rho=-(\rho+P)\,dV.$ Using $P=w\rho$, $V\,d\rho=-(1+w)\rho\,dV.$ Divide by $\rho V$: $\frac{d\rho}{\rho}=-(1+w)\frac{dV}{V}.$ Integrating, $\rho \propto V^{-(1+w)}.$ For a comoving cosmological box, $V\propto a^3,$ and therefore $\rho \propto a^{-3(1+w)}.$

p.src: Vacuum Energy and Negative Pressure

u.src: Vacuum Energy and Negative Pressure
en: Vacuum Energy and Negative Pressure

p.src: One special case behaves differently: $w=-1.$ Then $1+w=0,$ so the exponent vanishes and $\rho=\rho_0=\text{constant}.$ The corresponding pressure is $P=-\rho .$

p.src: Negative pressure is not mysterious in itself. Positive pressure pushes outward on the walls of a box. Negative pressure pulls inward. It is tension. A stretched rubber band gives the everyday example: it stores positive energy, but it pulls its ends together.

p.src: Substitute the constant density $\rho_0$ into the Friedmann equation: $\left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_0.$ The right-hand side is just a number, so $\frac{\dot a}{a}=\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_0}.$ This is the special case in which the Hubble quantity really is constant. The equation can be written as $\dot a=\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_0}\,a,$ and the solution is $a(t)\propto \exp\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho_0}\,t\right).$

p.src: Three Eras and the Observed Expansion History

u.src: Three Eras and the Observed Expansion History
en: Three Eras and the Observed Expansion History

p.src:
All three components are present, and they scale differently: $\begin{aligned}
\rho_{\text{radiation}}&\propto a^{-4},\\
\rho_{\text{matter}}&\propto a^{-3},\\
\rho_0&=\text{constant}.
\end{aligned}$ That immediately implies three eras.

a(t)\sim e^{Ht}.$

p.src: The rough times quoted here are these: radiation gives way to matter after about $10^4$ years. The universe becomes transparent later, after about $10^5$ years. The transition from matter domination to accelerated expansion occurs much later, after several billion years, roughly halfway through cosmic history in the order-of-magnitude estimate being used.

p.src: How is this history inferred? We cannot see the future, but we can see the past. Looking to greater distance means looking to earlier time. By observing distant galaxies, measuring how their motion correlates with distance, and reconstructing the Hubble quantity as a function of lookback time, one reconstructs the time history of the scale factor. The radiation-dominated era is too early to be seen directly in ordinary galaxy astronomy, but the matter-dominated era and the transition to vacuum domination are visible in the reconstructed curve.

By observing distant galaxies, measuring how their motion correlates with distance, and reconstructing the Hubble quantity as a function of lookback time, one reconstructs the time history of the scale factor. The radiation-dominated era is too early to be seen directly in ordinary galaxy astronomy, but the matter-dominated era and the transition to vacuum domination are visible in the reconstructed curve.

p.src: The important point is the late-time behavior. Once the expansion is exponential, the horizon distance becomes fixed. Galaxies continue to pass through it and disappear by becoming more and more redshifted. The microwave background is redshifted away as well. In the remote future, only the nearby gravitationally bound structures remain visible, and the universe looks like an isolated island.

p.src: The observational importance of $w$ is now clear. If astronomers report that $w$ is very close to $-1$, they are saying that the vacuum-energy component is very nearly constant. That is exactly the point made here.

p.src: That does not mean general relativity forces $w$ to be exactly $-1$. The point here is empirical. The lecture briefly notes that more radical possibilities are not excluded in principle, but that the nearly constant vacuum-energy case is the one for which there is good reason to believe.
